WORK.title: Mark
WORK.subtitle: This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God
intro: Mark is the shortest and fastest-moving of the four Gospels. It opens with John the Baptist crying out in the wilderness and, with almost no preamble, brings the reader to Jesus' side: calling disciples, healing the sick, driving out unclean spirits, calming the storm...

Mark keeps the story moving with words like "immediately" and "at once", like a documentary whose camera never stops. The whole book keeps asking one question: "Who is this man?" Until the centurion at the foot of the cross says: "Truly this man was the Son of God!"

matthew.title: Matthew
matthew.subtitle: The King of the kingdom of heaven
intro: Matthew is the first book of the New Testament. It opens with a family tree: a descendant of Abraham, a son of David, counted generation by generation down to Jesus, telling the reader that the promises of the Old Testament are fulfilled here.

Matthew writes for readers who know the Old Testament well and often says, "This was to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet." Five long discourses (the Sermon on the Mount, the sending of the Twelve, the parables of the kingdom, life among the disciples, and the teaching on the Mount of Olives) portray Jesus as the King and Teacher of the kingdom of heaven. The book opens with "Immanuel" and closes with "surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age."

luke.title: Luke
luke.subtitle: The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost
intro: Luke is the third book of the New Testament. Its author, Luke, was a physician who says he "carefully investigated everything from the beginning" and wrote an orderly account for Theophilus: it begins at the altar of incense in the temple with the old priest Zechariah, and ends with the disciples praising God in the temple.

Luke pays special attention to people others overlooked: shepherds, widows, tax collectors, Samaritans, a prodigal son and a criminal. Many stories are recorded only by Luke: the shepherds at the manger, the Good Samaritan, the lost sheep, the lost coin and the prodigal son, Zacchaeus, the criminal who repented on the cross, and the road to Emmaus. The thread running through the book is "the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost."

john.title: John
john.subtitle: The Word became flesh
intro: John is the fourth book of the New Testament. Its author is John, the disciple whom Jesus loved. He begins with "In the beginning was the Word" and records seven signs and the words Jesus spoke of Himself: "I am the bread of life," "I am the light of the world," "I am the good shepherd," "I am the resurrection and the life."

John records much that the other three Gospels do not: water turned into wine at the wedding in Cana, Nicodemus coming to Jesus at night, the Samaritan woman at the well, Lazarus walking out of the tomb, the night Jesus washed the disciples' feet in the upper room, and "Mary" spoken in the garden at dawn. The thread running through the whole book is life and light: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name."

acts.title: Acts
acts.subtitle: The gospel to the ends of the earth
intro: Acts is the fifth book of the New Testament and the sequel to the Gospel of Luke. Its author, Luke, begins with Jesus' ascension and records the Holy Spirit coming at Pentecost, as the disciples set out from Jerusalem to be His witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

The first half follows Peter: the lame man at the Beautiful Gate leaping up to walk, Stephen's martyrdom, Philip baptizing the Ethiopian official on the desert road, and Cornelius's household receiving the Holy Spirit. The second half follows Paul, the persecutor who became an apostle: three missionary journeys, songs at midnight in the Philippian jail, his address on the Areopagus in Athens, fourteen days of storm at sea, and at last Rome, where he boldly proclaimed the kingdom of God.

romans.title: Romans
romans.subtitle: Justified by faith
intro: Romans is Paul's letter to the believers in Rome. He had not yet been to Rome. Wintering in Corinth at the home of Gaius, he dictated it to Tertius, who wrote it down, and Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchrea, carried it across the sea.

This comic sets the whole letter in two places. By an evening lamp in Corinth, Paul paces as he speaks it line by line; in the workshop at the home of Priscilla and Aquila in Rome, a room of Jews and Gentiles hears it read aloud before dawn. They bow their heads at “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,” and look up at “justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” As the reading reaches “The night is nearly over; the day has drawn near,” the first light of morning slips in through the door.

corinthians1.title: 1 Corinthians
corinthians1.subtitle: Love is patient
intro: 1 Corinthians is Paul's letter from Ephesus to the church in Corinth. Some from Chloe's household had reported “there are quarrels among you,” and the Corinthians themselves had written with questions, so Paul answers them one by one: factions, lawsuits, marriage, food sacrificed to idols, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts, and the resurrection.

This comic sets the whole letter in two places. In the workshop of Aquila and Priscilla in Ephesus, Paul dictates over several early mornings while Sosthenes writes it down; in the courtyard of Gaius's house in Corinth, a roomful of divided people listens from afternoon deep into the night. When the reading reaches “the greatest of these is love,” the whole room lifts their faces; at “Where, O Death, is your victory?” golden light falls a second time under a sky full of stars.

corinthians2.title: 2 Corinthians
corinthians2.subtitle: Power made perfect in weakness
intro: 2 Corinthians is Paul's second letter to the church in Corinth, written from Macedonia. At Troas he could not find Titus, so he crossed the sea to Macedonia, where there were “conflicts on the outside, fears within,” until Titus came back from Corinth with news of the Corinthians' longing and zeal. The letter holds comfort and reconciliation, the collection for the saints in Jerusalem, and a heavy-hearted answer to those who looked down on him.

This comic sets the whole letter in two places. In the upper room of Lydia's house in Philippi, Paul dictates from a grey late-autumn day, to the first warm light when Titus arrives, to a single lamp on another evening, while Timothy writes it down. In the courtyard of Gaius's house in Corinth, Titus reads from early morning until noon; when he reaches “My grace is sufficient for you,” golden light falls on a tearful face lifted up beneath the lamp.

galatians.title: Galatians
galatians.subtitle: Freedom in Christ
intro: Galatians is Paul's urgent letter to the churches of Galatia. Visitors had come telling the disciples around Lystra that believing in Christ was not enough—they must also be circumcised and keep the law—and the believers were wavering. Paul begins with “I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel”: no thanksgiving, no long greetings. At the end he takes the pen himself and finishes in large letters with his own hand.

This comic sets the whole letter in two places. In a large house of the church in Antioch of Syria, Paul dictates under the hard white light of late summer while Titus writes it down; when he reaches “I no longer live, but Christ lives in me,” the light turns gold. In a dirt courtyard by the gate of Lystra, an elder reads from a windy, overcast afternoon until dusk. People who once watched Paul being stoned sit listening there, and the child of a slave runs into the father's arms, crying “Abba.”
Each chapter is adapted from Galatians in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

ephesians.title: Ephesians
ephesians.subtitle: The Body of Christ
intro: Ephesians is the letter Paul wrote as a prisoner in Rome, a chain linking him to the soldier who guarded him. There is nothing in it to rebuke: the first three chapters are one long song of praise and prayer—the dead are made alive, and the wall between the Gentiles and Israel is torn down; the last three are about living together—unity, putting off the old self, husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and slaves at home, and finally “the full armor of God.”

This comic sets the whole letter in two places. In a rented house in Rome, Paul dictates from early morning until dusk while Tychicus writes it down; when he reaches “it is by grace you have been saved through faith,” the light from the high window turns gold. In the lecture hall of Tyrannus in Ephesus, the elders read from noon until sunset. Those who once burned their books sit by the door holding empty chests, and Trophimus—the man on whose account Paul was seized—sits alone at the very edge.
Each chapter is adapted from Ephesians in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

philippians.title: Philippians
philippians.subtitle: Rejoice in the Lord Always
intro: Philippians is the letter Paul wrote in chains in Rome to the first church he had planted in Europe. He did not yet know whether he would live or die, yet the letter is full of joy: “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” At its center is the hymn of Christ who emptied Himself—though He existed in the form of God, He took the form of a servant and became obedient to death. It ends with “Rejoice in the Lord always,” and “I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.”

This comic sets the whole letter in two places. In a rented house in Rome, Paul dictates in chains while Timothy writes it down, and Epaphroditus, only just recovered from his illness, sits in the corner. In the courtyard of Lydia’s house in Philippi, the former jailer stands under the colonnade and reads the letter aloud; when he reaches “every knee should bow,” the whole courtyard kneels in golden light. Euodia and Syntyche, two sisters who could not agree, begin at opposite ends of the courtyard, and both look up at the same moment when their names are read.
Each chapter is adapted from Philippians in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

colossians.title: Colossians
colossians.subtitle: Christ, Supreme over All
intro: Colossians is the letter Paul wrote in chains in Rome to a church he had never visited. The gospel had been carried home to the Lycus Valley by Epaphras, one of their own, and now some there were teaching “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!” Paul does not scold. The whole letter speaks of how great one Person is: “in Him all things were created,” and “He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together.” So they are to be rooted and built up in Him, to put off the old self and put on the new, and “whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord.”

This comic sets the whole letter in two places. In a rented house in Rome, Paul dictates in chains while Timothy writes it down; Epaphras sits across from them, and later kneels in the corner, wrestling in prayer for them. In the courtyard of a house in Colossae, Tychicus reads the letter from morning until the lamps are lit, with Onesimus, a man of that city, standing half a step behind him. When he reaches “in Him all things hold together,” golden light spills down from the snowy peaks and the whole courtyard lifts its face.
Each chapter is adapted from Colossians in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

thessalonians1.title: 1 Thessalonians
thessalonians1.subtitle: The Hope of the Lord's Return
intro: 1 Thessalonians is Paul's earliest letter. He had preached in Thessalonica for only three Sabbaths before the brothers sent him out of the city by night; by the time he reached Corinth, Timothy came back with the news: the believers there had not scattered. The letter holds no rebuke, only longing: “like a nursing mother caring for her children.” It also answers the thing that hurt them most. Some among them had fallen asleep, and those still living were grieving “like the rest, who are without hope.” Paul tells them that when the Lord comes, “we will always be with the Lord.” It closes with a string of short charges: “Rejoice at all times. Pray without ceasing. Give thanks in every circumstance.”

This comic sets the whole letter in two places. In Aquila's workshop in Corinth, Paul dictates with a tentmaker's needle still in his hand, Silas writes it down, and Timothy, just back from the road, sits beside them. In Jason's house in Thessalonica, behind a door once kicked in and now nailed with fresh boards, the letter is read by lamplight before dawn. Among the listeners are a potter who carried the little clay idols out of his house, and a widow who has just buried her husband, holding a small boy by the hand. When the reading reaches the Lord's coming, the sun rises out of the sea, golden light floods the room, and every face lifts.

Each chapter is adapted from 1 Thessalonians in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

thessalonians2.title: 2 Thessalonians
thessalonians2.subtitle: Stand Firm in What You Were Taught
intro: 2 Thessalonians was written from Corinth by Paul, Silas, and Timothy not long after the first letter was sent. The persecution had not stopped, yet the letter opens by saying “your faith is growing more and more.” A letter was going around the city under Paul's name, claiming that the Day of the Lord had already come, and some were so shaken they had stopped working. Paul writes that they are “not to be easily disconcerted or alarmed,” and tells them to “stand firm.” To those who used waiting for the Lord as an excuse to sit idle and eat other people's bread, he speaks plainly: “If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat.” And he adds: “Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.”

This comic picks up from 1 Thessalonians in the same two places. In the workshop in Corinth, Paul dictates late at night with a needle between his fingers. In Jason's house in Thessalonica, one more fresh board has been nailed across the door, and at dusk people come in from work to hear the letter. When the reading reaches the Lord revealed from heaven in blazing fire, the sunset at the doorway lights up the lifted faces of the widow and the little boy. At the end, the potter puts a lump of wet clay into the idle man's hands, and that night guides his hands at the wheel as he learns to work it.

Each chapter is adapted from 2 Thessalonians in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

timothy1.title: 1 Timothy
timothy1.subtitle: Order in the Church
intro: 1 Timothy is the letter Paul wrote after leaving for Macedonia, to Timothy, who had stayed behind in Ephesus. The Saul who once dragged people off to prison now writes to teach a young man how to keep a church: “This is a trustworthy saying, worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst.” The letter covers how to pray, how to choose overseers and deacons, and how to care for widows, because the church is “the pillar and foundation of the truth.” And to his young co-worker he says: “Let no one despise your youth,” and “Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life.”

This comic is set in two places. In the courtyard of Lydia's house in Philippi, where purple linen hangs drying, Paul writes the letter line by line in his own hand. In the lecture hall of Tyrannus in Ephesus, Timothy grips the scroll and reads from the very edge of the stone steps while someone in the front row snickers. From early morning to dusk, chapter by chapter, he makes his way to the middle of the steps, and a white-haired elder is the first to nod. The widow under the farthest pillar is taken home, and the last of the sunset fills the courtyard. At the end, in a small room at night, Timothy lays the letter in a wooden box and rests his hand on it.
Each chapter is adapted from 1 Timothy in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

timothy2.title: 2 Timothy
timothy2.subtitle: The Good Fight
intro: 2 Timothy is Paul's last letter. He is a prisoner in Rome for the second time: “For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand.” Winter is coming, and the people around him have scattered; “Only Luke is with me.” He writes “to Timothy, my beloved child”: “For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.” Though he himself is in chains, he says, “But the word of God cannot be chained!” He tells Timothy to hold on to the Scriptures he has known since childhood and to preach the word, and then: “Make every effort to come to me quickly.”

This comic is set in two places. In a small stone-walled room in Rome, Paul's chain is fastened to a ring in the wall and Luke writes for him; with each chapter the room grows colder and emptier. In a small room in Ephesus at night, Timothy reads the letter alone by lamplight. On the last night, a beam of golden light comes through the high window and falls on Paul's face: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” At the end, Timothy boards a ship with Mark, and the weather has already turned cold.
Each chapter is adapted from 2 Timothy in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

titus.title: Titus
titus.subtitle: Sound Teaching
intro: Titus is Paul's letter to his co-worker Titus, whom he had left on Crete: “The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you.” On the island some were undermining entire households “for the sake of dishonorable gain,” and even one of the Cretans' own prophets had said, “Cretans are always liars.” Yet Paul tells Titus, “But as for you, speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine,” because “the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone”: “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy.”

This comic is set in two places. In the inner courtyard of Lydia's house in Philippi, Paul writes from an autumn morning until the lamps are lit at dusk. In the courtyard of an old fisherman's house in a small harbor town on Crete, Titus stands under an old olive tree and reads the letter aloud: two elders are appointed, a young woman sitting alone on the steps by the gate is welcomed into the crowd, and the setting sun shines in from the sea through the gate. At the end, in the early-morning harbor, Titus sees Apollos and Zenas off on a ship, his own pack already tied up at his feet: “make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis.”
Each chapter is adapted from Titus in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

philemon.title: Philemon
philemon.subtitle: From Slave to Brother
intro: Philemon is a short letter Paul wrote while imprisoned in Rome to Philemon of Colossae. Philemon's slave Onesimus had left his master's house, met Paul in Rome, and come to faith; Paul calls him “my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains”: “Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me.” Paul could have ordered him, yet “I prefer to appeal on the basis of love”: take him back “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother.”

This comic is set in two places. In a rented house in Rome, Paul in chains dictates by lamplight at dusk and hands the letter to Tychicus; the next morning the little stool in the corner is empty. In the stone-paved courtyard of Philemon's house in Colossae, Philemon reads the letter on the porch steps with a smile, while Onesimus stands outside the half-open gate from beginning to end. The setting sun shines in through the gate, and Philemon lays down the scroll and comes down the steps to meet him: “So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me.”
This chapter is adapted from Philemon in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

hebrews.title: Hebrews
hebrews.subtitle: A Better Covenant
intro: Hebrews is a letter to people who had believed for a long time. In the early days they had suffered greatly for the Lord and even accepted the seizure of their property with joy; now the hard days dragged on. Some had stopped meeting together, and some wanted to go back to the priests, sacrifices, and temple rules they had known before. The writer does not scold; line by line he lifts their eyes from earth to heaven: in these last days God “has spoken to us by His Son.” He is greater than the angels and greater than Moses, a high priest in the order of Melchizedek who offered Himself once for all. “Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees.”

This comic is set in two places. In a small stone-walled room, a man whose face we never see writes the letter by an oil lamp. The letter travels to a room with its shutters closed and a single lamp lit, where a weary, frightened group gathers around the lamp and listens from nightfall until dawn. A middle-aged man with his hand on the door bolt and a young mother whose husband is in chains follow along page by page. When the reading reaches “we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses,” someone pushes open the wooden shutter and the morning light floods the room; at the end the door stands wide open, and they “go to Him outside the camp.”
Each chapter is adapted from Hebrews in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

james.title: James
james.subtitle: Faith and Deeds
intro: James is a letter from James, the Lord’s brother, “to the twelve tribes of the Dispersion.” Its first hearers were caught in trials of many kinds: in the synagogue some wore gold rings and some wore shabby clothes; the poor were dragged into court by the rich, and the workers who mowed the fields were cheated of their wages; people said they had faith, yet when they saw a brother or sister without clothes and food, they only said, “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed.” James does not give long arguments; every line lands on the hands and the mouth: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only”; “faith without deeds is dead”; “the tongue also is a fire”; “Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you.”

This comic is set in two places. In a stone house in Jerusalem, a man whose knees are calloused from kneeling rises from prayer and writes the letter. The letter travels to a synagogue in a small town far away and is read aloud on a hot, dry day to a full room—in the front, on soft cushions, sits a man with a gold ring; at the back by the door stand harvest workers just in from the fields. By the end of the letter, where people sit has changed; when the reading reaches “the prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail,” the man with the gold ring walks over and sits beside the workers, and the rain begins to fall.
Each chapter is adapted from James in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

peter1.title: 1 Peter
peter1.subtitle: Hope in Suffering
intro: 1 Peter is a letter the apostle Peter wrote from “Babylon” to “the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.” They had been Gentiles; after they believed, their old friends slandered them. In their households some were servants beaten by harsh masters, and some were wives whose husbands did not obey the word; “the fiery trial” was coming upon them. Peter’s first word is hope: “He has given us new birth into a living hope”; you are “foreigners and exiles,” yet you are also “a royal priesthood”; Christ also suffered, “leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps”; “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.”

This comic is set in two places. In a mud-brick house at dusk, a fisherman graying at the temples finishes dictating the letter and hands the scroll to Silvanus, who is setting out on a long journey. The letter reaches a courtyard in a mountain village on the high plateau, and after nightfall everyone gathers around a fire to listen—a young servant with whip wounds on his arm huddles in a corner, and a wife keeps glancing back at her husband standing outside the gate. The letter is read from nightfall until dawn; when the reading reaches “Cast all your anxiety on Him,” the servant lets go of the arm he has been clutching, and at sunrise he stands at the gate beside that husband.
Each chapter is adapted from 1 Peter in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

peter2.title: 2 Peter
peter2.subtitle: Grow and Stay Alert
intro: 2 Peter is the second letter written by “Simon Peter”: “Beloved, this is now my second letter to you.” The writer knows that “this tent will soon be laid aside,” so he will “always remind you of these things.” This time the danger comes from within: “there will be false teachers among you,” and they “feast with you”; outside there are scoffers who ask, “Where is the promise of His coming?” Peter answers: the prophetic word is “a lamp shining in a dark place”; “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials”; the Lord is not slow, but “is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.”

This comic is set in two places. On a winter night in a small house, the aged Peter, wrapped in an old blanket, dictates his last letter alone beside a lamp. The letter reaches the mountain village from 1 Peter and is read on a snowy night around a lamp in the elder’s stone house—a well-dressed guest who has often feasted with them these past months is there too, and the youngest of the young men has already taken a seat beside him. The letter is read from lamplight until dawn; in the middle of the night the young man comes back through the snow and finds the elder standing at the courtyard gate with a lamp, still waiting for him.
Each chapter is adapted from 2 Peter in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

john1.title: 1 John
john1.subtitle: God Is Love
intro: 1 John has no opening greeting and names neither its writer nor its readers; it reads like an old man speaking to people he has watched grow up: “My little children.” The writer says the Word of life is that “which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands.” The church receiving the letter has just been through something painful: “They went out from us, but they did not belong to us.” Again and again the letter returns to light and love: “God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all”; if anyone “sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him,” the letter says, “let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth”; because “God is love,” and “there is no fear in love.”

This comic is set in two places. In a small whitewashed house before dawn, a white-haired old man writes by lamplight with his own hand to the people he calls “little children.” The letter reaches a family courtyard in a small town—a house church that has just lost several of its people. A stretch of bench sits empty, and on the empty place stands a clay cup no one has cleared away; a brother with possessions sits alone on the innermost bench, while a poor brother sits barefoot on a straw mat by the courtyard gate. The letter is read from before dawn until dusk. At noon, when the reading reaches “anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen,” the brother with possessions stands up, crosses the courtyard, and goes to the straw mat; at dusk the lamps are lit under the porch, and the empty bench is full.
Each chapter is adapted from 1 John in comic form. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

john2.title: 2 John
john2.subtitle: Walking in the Truth
intro: 2 John has only thirteen verses. The writer calls himself “the elder” and writes “to the chosen lady and her children.” He says, “I was overjoyed to find some of your children walking in the truth, just as the Father has commanded us,” and urges her “that we love one another.” He also warns her: “many deceivers have gone out into the world”; “If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home.” At the end he says he has many more things to write, but would prefer not to use paper and ink: “I hope to come and speak with you face to face, so that our joy may be complete.”

This comic is set in two places. Early in the morning, in a small whitewashed house, a white-haired old man writes with his own hand while a young brother and sister grind the ink and trim the reed pens beside him. At dusk the letter reaches a flat-roofed stone house at the edge of town, where a lamp hangs on the doorframe for passing guests. While the lady reads the letter, her children are binding the feet of traveling brothers and setting out more bread; after dark someone knocks, and she stands in the doorway without stepping aside, the door lamp lighting the threshold between them; late at night she carries a small lamp to the door and, standing on tiptoe, turns up the lamp.
This comic adapts 2 John. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

john3.title: 3 John
john3.subtitle: Welcoming Those Who Serve the Gospel
intro: 3 John is a short letter to one man: “The elder, To the beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth.” Brothers came back and reported that Gaius was walking in the truth, and the writer says, “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.” Gaius welcomed the traveling brothers who preached, men who “went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles”; the letter tells him, “you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you.” In the same church, “Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction,” and he even puts out of the church those who welcome the brothers. The letter urges Gaius, “do not imitate what is evil, but what is good,” and says that Demetrius “has received a good testimony from everyone.” At the end: “Greet each of our friends there by name.”

This comic is set around two doors. In a small hillside town, the wooden door of Gaius’s house always stands open to the street, and a wooden rack beside it holds the walking staffs of passing brothers. In the afternoon women wash the travelers’ feet while Gaius stuffs bread into their packs; early in the morning at the town gate, he hands his own staff to the last man setting out. At another meeting house in the same town, a heavy door shuts in the travelers’ faces, and the rack beside it stands empty. At dusk one door is lit and the other dark; far away, in a small whitewashed house, a white-haired old man sets down his pen and reaches for the old walking stick in the corner.
This comic adapts 3 John. The English edition quotes Scripture word for word from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB); added dialogue and narration are marked separately.

jude.title: Jude
jude.subtitle: Contend for the Faith
intro: Jude is a short, urgent letter from “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James.” He had meant to write about the salvation we share, but “I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints,” because “certain men have crept in among you unnoticed,” men who “turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality.” The letter lines up warnings from the Old Testament: the people who did not believe after leaving Egypt, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam, and Korah; at the love feasts these men are “clouds without water” and “fruitless trees in autumn.” At the end it urges the readers to keep “praying in the Holy Spirit” and to “keep yourselves in the love of God,” and to “have mercy on those who doubt.” The letter closes in praise: “Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling.”

This comic is set in two places. Early in the morning, in a stone house, the gray-haired writer sits alone at a small east window; halfway through, he rises to his feet, the reed pen still in his hand. The letter reaches a large courtyard in the countryside, where a love feast is held at night around a long lamp-lit table, and an elder reads it aloud. A side door opens a crack, and three well-dressed men slip into seats at the far end of the table. A young man holding a piece of bread is waved over to them and laughs along, until he sees them whispering at the corner of the table and his laughter stops; the elder sets down the scroll, walks over, and lays a hand on his shoulder. When the reading reaches the final praise, the whole courtyard rises together and looks up.

revelation.title: Revelation
revelation.subtitle: A New Heaven and a New Earth
intro: Revelation is the last book of the New Testament. The aged John “was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus.” On the Lord’s day he heard a loud voice behind him: “Write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches.” He saw one like the Son of Man among seven golden lampstands and fell at His feet like a dead man; but He placed His right hand on him and said, “Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last.” Then He spoke to the seven churches one by one: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock.” Next a door stood open in heaven: the throne, the scroll sealed with seven seals, and a new song, “Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain.” Seven seals, seven trumpets, and seven bowls come down one after another; the dragon and the beasts, and the great city Babylon, all fall. At last come a new heaven and a new earth, and the holy city coming down out of heaven: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,” and the One seated on the throne said, “Behold, I make all things new.” The book ends with a prayer: “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!”

The comic begins on the rocky shore of Patmos: gray-brown volcanic rock, a deep blue sea, and old John with white hair and beard, leaning on a worn staff and spreading a leather scroll on a flat stone. Each vision opens out beside him and comes back to him again: he falls down, weeps loudly, eats the little scroll, and twice falls on his face and is raised up. The visions are drawn as large and fierce as the text: full-page panels, spreads where two pages join into one picture, and one main color for each section—the blazing white of the Son of Man, the rainbow of the throne, the fiery red of the trumpets, the dark red and black of the dragon and the beasts, the purple and gold of Babylon—until the New Jerusalem unfolds the book’s only great sweep of warm gold. The last page returns to early morning on Patmos, where old John lifts his face on the shore.

genesis.title: Genesis
genesis.subtitle: In the Beginning
intro: Genesis is the first book of the Bible. “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light; in six days He made all things, created man in His own image, and saw that all He had made was very good. Then come the garden of Eden, the serpent and the fruit, Cain and Abel, the flood and the rainbow, and the tower of Babel. God calls Abraham to leave his country and promises that his offspring will be as many as the stars of the sky; on Mount Moriah Abraham offers up Isaac—“The LORD Will Provide.” Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph follow one generation after another, until Joseph tells his brothers, “As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good.”

The comic draws each scene with the weight the text gives it: creation unfolds in great full-page scenes, with light bursting out of the heart of the darkness; the offering of Isaac is a quiet, emotional chapter in which father and son climb the mountain with hardly a word.

exodus.title: Exodus
exodus.subtitle: God Rescues His People
intro: Exodus tells how God brought the Israelites out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. From the fire in the burning bush God calls Moses; ten plagues fall on Egypt, and the blood of the Passover is put on the doorframes. Pharaoh’s chariots chase the people to the sea; Moses stretches out his staff, and they go through the sea on dry ground, “with walls of water on their right and on their left.” At Mount Sinai God gives the Ten Commandments and tells the people to build the tabernacle, and His glory fills it.

joshua.title: Joshua
joshua.subtitle: Into the Promised Land
intro: Joshua begins after the death of Moses, when God tells Joshua, “Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged.” On the wall of Jericho, Rahab ties a scarlet cord in her window. As soon as the priests carrying the ark step into the water, the Jordan, flooding all its banks, stands up in a heap far upstream, and the people cross on dry ground. For seven days they march around the city in silence; on the seventh day the horns sound, the people shout, and the wall collapses—only Rahab’s stretch of wall is left standing. Then come the defeat at Ai, Achan’s sin, and the sun standing still over Gibeon, and the whole land is divided among the twelve tribes: “Not one of the LORD’s good promises to the house of Israel had failed.” At the end, at Shechem, the white-haired Joshua rises and says, “As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”

The first half of the comic draws the battles—the wall of water, the city wall, the hailstones—with the weight the text gives them; the second half divides the land on a single map of Canaan, coloring in one tribe’s portion chapter by chapter.

judges.title: Judges
judges.subtitle: God Raises Up Deliverers
intro: Judges begins after the death of Joshua. The tribes do not drive out the Canaanites, and “another generation rose up who did not know the LORD.” So the same cycle turns again and again—Israel does evil, is handed over to its enemies, cries out, and “the LORD raised up judges, who saved them from the hands of those who plundered them.” Left-handed Ehud, Deborah under her palm tree, Jael in her tent; Gideon, threshing wheat in a winepress, hears “The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor,” and three hundred men shatter their jars and lift their torches; Jephthah’s daughter dances out the door with her tambourine; Samson’s hair is shaved and then “began to grow back,” and in the temple of Dagon he prays, “Please remember me.” The last chapters grow darker and darker, and the final line is: “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”

The comic paints the hillside where Israel bows to Baal seven times, and the village at rest four times, from the same camera angle; each chapter is darker than the one before, after Gideon there are no more sunny days of rest, and the last panel of the book is an empty stone bench at the city gate in the dusk.

ruth.title: Ruth
ruth.subtitle: Loyal and Redeeming Love
intro: “In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land,” and a family of four from Bethlehem goes down to Moab; ten years later only three widows are left. On the road home Orpah kisses her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth the Moabitess clings to her: “For wherever you go, I will go … your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.” Back in town Naomi says, “Do not call me Naomi. Call me Mara … I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.” Ruth goes out to glean and “happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz,” who tells her, “May you receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge.” At night on the threshing floor she asks, “Spread the corner of your garment over me.” Ten elders bear witness at the city gate, Boaz marries Ruth, and the neighbor women say, “A son has been born to Naomi”—“He became the father of Jesse, the father of David.”

The comic follows the darkness of Judges but turns the other way, growing brighter chapter by chapter: Naomi’s two hands are painted four times from the same angle, empty, then holding an ephah of barley, then six measures of barley, and at last the child in her lap; the empty stone bench at the gate in the dusk at the end of Judges fills up here, one seat at a time, in the morning light; there are no miracles in the book, and God’s hand is hidden in the composition.

The boy Samuel hears God calling him in the sanctuary and answers, “Speak, for Your servant is listening.” The people ask for a king; Saul is anointed but does not obey the word of God, so God sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint Jesse’s youngest son, the shepherd David. In the Valley of Elah the young David goes out against the giant Goliath with a sling and five smooth stones: “I come against you in the name of the LORD of Hosts.”

samuel2.title: 2 Samuel
samuel2.subtitle: David Reigns
intro: 2 Samuel begins in the ruins of Ziklag. David hears that Saul and Jonathan are dead and laments them in the Song of the Bow: “How the mighty have fallen!” He reigns first over Judah in Hebron, then captures the fortress of Zion, brings the ark of God into Jerusalem, and dances with all his might before the LORD. Through the prophet Nathan, God promises him, “Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me.” But one evening David strolls on the roof of the palace, and afterward Nathan tells him, “You are that man!” From then on the sword never departs from his house. Absalom rises to seize the throne, and David weeps in the chamber over the gate: “O my son Absalom!” At the end of the book he builds an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah, and the plague is halted.

The comic draws each scene with the weight the text gives it: in the first half David grows ever brighter and stands ever nearer the center of the frame; after that one evening in chapter 11, the same man is pushed to the edges and into the shadows. Only two moments in the book are lit with warm gold: the promise Nathan brings to David, and David’s last words, “like the light of the morning at sunrise of a cloudless dawn.”

kings1.title: 1 Kings
kings1.subtitle: Solomon and the Divided Kingdom
intro: 1 Kings opens in David’s old age. As the king nears death, he charges Solomon to be strong and to walk in the ways of the LORD. At Gibeon Solomon asks God in a dream for wisdom, and with a single sword he settles the case of two women fighting over one child. In seven years he builds the temple; the ark is carried into the Most Holy Place, and the cloud fills the house of the LORD. But the king’s heart turns away, and under his son the kingdom splits in two, north and south. King follows king, most of them doing evil in the sight of the LORD. Then Elijah the Tishbite steps out of Gilead: ravens by the brook, the widow’s jar at Zarephath, fire falling on Mount Carmel while the people fall on their faces and confess that the LORD is God. And on Mount Horeb, after the wind, the earthquake, and the fire, comes a quiet, gentle voice.

The comic draws each scene with the weight the text gives it: the first half grows ever fuller—cedar, gold, the bronze sea—and the cloud filling the temple is the brightest panel in the book; the second half grows ever emptier—a dry brook, an empty jar, a mountain, the mouth of a cave.

kings2.title: 2 Kings
kings2.subtitle: The Rise and Fall of Two Kingdoms
intro: 2 Kings opens with a chariot of fire: as Elijah and Elisha walk along talking, chariots and horses of fire separate the two, and Elijah goes up to heaven in a whirlwind. Elisha picks up the cloak that fell from him and strikes the Jordan. Then come Elisha’s miracles, most of them in the homes of the poor: a widow’s oil poured out jar after jar, a Shunammite woman’s son who sneezes seven times and opens his eyes, the Aramean commander Naaman dipping seven times in the Jordan. After that, king follows king, and the northern kingdom falls before Assyria. In the south, Hezekiah spreads Assyria’s letter out before the LORD, and Josiah, hearing the Book of the Law found in the temple, tears his clothes. Yet in the end Jerusalem is burned and the people are carried off to Babylon.

The comic draws each scene with the weight the text gives it: the first half is warm, close, and small—an oil jar, an upper room, a pot, an axe head; the second half grows ever farther and emptier, until the last warm color is the fire that burns the temple. The book ends with one small lamp: Jehoiachin, thirty-seven years an exile, is released from prison and eats at the table of the king of Babylon.

ezra.title: Ezra
ezra.subtitle: Returning to Rebuild the Temple
intro: 2 Kings ends with exile to Babylon; Ezra begins with the road home. The LORD stirs the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, who decrees that the people of Judah may go up to Jerusalem and build the house of the LORD, and the treasurer counts out, one by one, the gold and silver articles Nebuchadnezzar had carried away—5,400 in all. More than forty-two thousand people walk west to the ruins. They set up the altar on its old foundation, then lay the foundation of the temple: the old men who had seen the first temple weep aloud, the young shout for joy, and “the people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping.” Letters of accusation stop the work for years, until the prophets Haggai and Zechariah speak; King Darius finds Cyrus’s scroll in the fortress of Ecbatana, and at last the temple is finished. More than fifty years later the scribe Ezra comes up with the Book of the Law: “Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel.” When he hears that the people have intermarried with the nations, he tears his garments, kneels before the temple, and spreads out his hands in prayer; the whole assembly sits before the house of God in the heavy rain and confesses.

The comic draws each scene with the weight the text gives it: the book has no great miracles and no battles, and its big scenes are all people—a long column walking west, a foundation where weeping and shouting cannot be told apart, a dark crowd in the rain. Three panels drawn from the same angle—the foundation laid, grass growing over it while the work stands still, the temple finished—are the book’s timeline; “the hand of God” is never drawn as a hand, only as a beam of morning light on the road.

nehemiah.title: Nehemiah
nehemiah.subtitle: Rebuilding the Walls of Jerusalem
intro: Ezra rebuilt the temple; Nehemiah rebuilds the wall. In the palace at Susa, the king’s cupbearer Nehemiah hears that the wall of Jerusalem is broken down and its gates burned with fire; he sits down and weeps, fasting and praying. Before the king he cannot hide his sadness, and he prays silently before he answers. At night he rides around the burned walls on his animal, then tells the people, “Let us start rebuilding”—more than forty sections of wall, each family repairing the stretch in front of its own house. Sanballat and Tobiah mock and plot an attack, so the laborers “worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other,” and the trumpeter stands beside Nehemiah. When the poor cry out that their children are being sold as slaves, Nehemiah is angry and makes the nobles give back their fields. “So the wall was completed in fifty-two days, on the twenty-fifth of Elul.” With the wall standing, Ezra reads the Book of the Law from a wooden platform; the people weep, and they hear that “the joy of the LORD is your strength.” They fast and confess, sign a binding covenant, and two thanksgiving choirs march toward each other along the top of the wall. Twelve years later Nehemiah returns to find Tobiah living in a room in the temple and fish being sold at the gates on the Sabbath—and the book ends with one short prayer: “Remember me, O my God, with favor.”

The comic draws each scene with the weight the text gives it: Nehemiah is a man of action—sleeves rolled up, hands gray with mortar, a short sword at his belt—while Ezra is a man of the book, always holding a scroll; when they share a panel, one moves and one is still. A bird’s-eye view of Jerusalem’s whole circuit of walls is drawn several times from the same angle—half built, fully lit after fifty-two days, two processions walking toward each other on top—and serves as the book’s map. Each time Nehemiah prays silently, he is drawn halfway through some task, looking up for a moment as light falls from above; the last panel of the book is that same moment.

esther.title: Esther
esther.subtitle: A Queen for Such a Time as This
intro: The book of Esther never once mentions the name of God. In Susa, King Xerxes displays the wealth of his kingdom for a hundred and eighty days and holds a seven-day banquet; Queen Vashti refuses to come and is deposed. Young women are gathered from across the empire, and Esther—a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai—is taken into the palace and crowned queen without telling anyone who she is. At the king’s gate Mordecai overhears two eunuchs plotting against the king; it is recorded in the royal chronicles, then forgotten. Haman is promoted, and “All the royal servants at the king’s gate bowed down and paid homage to Haman … But Mordecai would not bow down or pay homage.” The Pur is cast to choose a day to destroy all the Jews; the king hands Haman his signet ring, and “the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion.” Mordecai, in sackcloth and ashes, sends word to Esther: “And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” She answers, “And if I perish, I perish!” On the third day she enters the inner court unbidden, and the king extends the gold scepter. “That night sleep escaped the king”; the records read to him are the very account of Mordecai saving his life—so Haman leads Mordecai through the streets on the king’s horse, and at Esther’s second banquet he is exposed: “this wicked man—Haman!” An edict sealed with the king’s ring cannot be revoked, so a second one is written, and on the appointed day “the Jews overpowered those who hated them.” The book ends with Purim, the month “in which their sorrow turned to joy and their mourning into a holiday,” with gifts sent to one another and to the poor.

The comic draws each scene with the weight the text gives it. No light from heaven appears anywhere in the book; God’s hand is hidden in things that simply happen—Mordecai happening to overhear two shadows in a gateway, a volume of the chronicles closed and left to gather dust, and that same volume opened on the king’s sleepless night. Nearly every image in the first half has a mirror panel from the same angle in the second: the king pulls off his ring for Haman, and later for Mordecai; couriers ride out of the city twice with an edict; when the whole court bows to Haman only one back stands upright, and later, on the same street, it is Haman leading the horse. Esther is drawn step by step, from lowered eyes and a headscarf folded away at the bottom of a chest to the moment she rises and speaks of “my people.” A cast lot lies in the corner of every date panel, and the last panel of the book is that same lot.

jonah.title: Jonah
jonah.subtitle: The Great Fish and Nineveh
intro: Jonah was a prophet of the northern kingdom in the days of Jeroboam II (he has already appeared in 2 Kings 14:25). The word of the LORD comes to him: “Get up! Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it”—Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, the enemy Israel feared most. “Jonah, however, got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD,” and his road runs downward: down to Joppa, down into a ship, down into the hold to sleep. The LORD sends a great wind on the sea; the foreign sailors each cry out to their own god, and the captain shakes him awake: “How can you sleep? Get up and call upon your God.” The lot falls on Jonah, and he says, “I am a Hebrew … I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land.” He tells the sailors to throw him into the sea, and the sea grows calm; the first to fear the LORD and offer Him sacrifices and vows are those foreigners. “Now the LORD had appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of the fish”; from the depths he prays, “Salvation is from the LORD!” The word comes a second time; he goes, and in the city he cries out a single sentence: “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!” The whole city, from the king down to the cattle, puts on sackcloth, and God relents from the disaster. But Jonah is furious: “This is why I was so quick to flee toward Tarshish. I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God …” God appoints a plant to shade him, then a worm to wither it, and Jonah says, “I am angry enough to die!” The book ends on a question from God—“So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh, which has more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many cattle as well?”—and Jonah’s answer is never given.

The comic draws each scene with the weight the text gives it. Through the first half Jonah is always going down, the composition slanting from upper left to lower right—down the harbor steps, down into the hold, sinking into the sea—until the fish spits him onto dry land and, for the first time, the camera looks up at him from below. The LORD “appoints” four times—a fish, a plant, a worm, an east wind—and each time the comic only shows that thing entering from a corner of the panel, with no light from heaven. The irony is left to paired panels: on deck the sailors cry out to their gods while below the prophet sleeps; the raised hands of the sailors making their vows to the LORD return in the fish as Jonah, in the same pose, says “I will fulfill what I have vowed”; Nineveh, from the king down to the donkeys, puts on sackcloth, and the next page holds Jonah’s angriest face in the book. Inside the city the comic follows one ordinary bricklayer’s family, and the last panel of the book does not show Jonah’s face at all—it returns to the child at that family’s door who cannot tell his right hand from his left, and leaves the question for the reader to answer.

ezekiel.title: Ezekiel
ezekiel.subtitle: The Dry Bones Live
intro: Ezekiel, son of the priest Buzi, was carried off to Babylon in the same deportation as King Jehoiachin and lived by the River Kebar—more than a thousand kilometers from Jerusalem, while Jeremiah was still prophesying inside the city. The exiles thought God had stayed behind in Jerusalem, but “while I was among the exiles by the River Kebar, the heavens opened and I saw visions of God”: in a whirlwind from the north, four living creatures, a wheel within a wheel full of eyes, and around the throne a brilliance like a rainbow in the clouds—“This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell facedown.” God has him eat a scroll written with lament, “So I ate, and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth,” and says, “Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel.” For years afterward he barely speaks and preaches with his body: he draws a besieged city on a brick, lies on his left side for three hundred ninety days, shaves his hair and divides it in three, and digs through a wall at night carrying his bags. The Spirit carries him back to Jerusalem, where he sees creeping things carved on the temple walls and elders holding censers, and then watches as “the glory of the LORD moved away from the threshold of the temple,” step by step eastward, until it “stood over the mountain east of the city.” His wife dies suddenly and God forbids him to mourn—the day the city falls will come on them the same way. “A fugitive from Jerusalem came to me and reported, ‘The city has been taken!’” That day his mouth is opened, and the message turns from judgment to restoration: “I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh.” On a valley full of bones God asks, “Son of man, can these bones come to life?”—“and the breath entered them, and they came to life and stood on their feet—a vast army.” The last nine chapters are a vision of a new temple: “the glory of the LORD entered the temple through the gate facing east,” and from under its threshold a river flows, deeper and deeper—“wherever the river flows, everything will flourish.” The book ends on the name of a city: “THE LORD IS THERE.”

The comic draws each scene with the weight the text gives it. The visions are drawn stroke by stroke from the text—four faces, four wings, feet gleaming like polished bronze, wheels full of eyes, a crystal expanse, a sapphire throne—and the One on the throne is drawn only as a glow of gleaming metal and fire ringed by a rainbow, never as a human figure. Ezekiel is so often “brought to see” that many panels look over his shoulder: his back in the foreground, the reader seeing with him. Three panels from the same camera angle hold the whole book together: the glory pausing at the temple’s east gate, leaving the city to stand on the mountain to the east, and more than thirty chapters later returning through that same east gate to fill the temple. His sign-acts are drawn as real events, and the faces of the watching exiles—sneering, then used to it, then asking—are a mirror for the reader; his wife appears in only two panels, and the second is a folded deep indigo headscarf on a bed at dawn. The valley of bones is anchored by the same slanting rock across four panels: bone joining bone, sinews and flesh, a covering of rough cloth, standing up in the morning wind. The water from under the temple is four panels from one angle too—ankle-deep, knee-deep, waist-deep, a river—until the Dead Sea turns emerald and fishermen spread their nets along the shore.

hosea.title: Hosea
hosea.subtitle: Unfailing Love
intro: Hosea was the son of Beeri, a man of the northern kingdom of Israel. He spoke in the days when Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah reigned in Judah and Jeroboam son of Jehoash reigned in Israel—the north was rich, with palaces inlaid with ivory, hills covered in vineyards, and a golden calf on the altar at Bethel; within forty years Samaria would fall. The first thing the LORD said to him was startling: “Go, take a prostitute as your wife and have children of adultery, because this land is flagrantly prostituting itself by departing from the LORD.” “So Hosea went and married Gomer daughter of Diblaim.” Three children were born one after another, and every name was a judgment: Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah (“No Compassion”), and Lo-ammi (“Not My People”). Gomer left home to pursue her lovers, “but not catch them,” and then said, “I will return to my first husband, for then I was better off than now.” God said, “I will allure her and lead her to the wilderness, and speak to her tenderly,” and “make the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope”; “I will betroth you to Me forever.” Then comes the hardest line in the book: “Go show love to your wife again, though she is loved by another and is an adulteress. Love her as the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods.” Hosea says, “So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley.” From chapter 4 on, the prophet speaks to the whole northern kingdom: “There is no truth, no loving devotion, and no knowledge of God in the land!” “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.” “For your loyalty is like a morning mist, like the early dew that vanishes.” “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.” “For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind.” Yet in the middle of the words of judgment, God’s heart turns again and again: “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son.” “It was I who taught Ephraim to walk.” “I led them with cords of kindness, with ropes of love.” “How could I give you up, O Ephraim? How could I surrender you, O Israel? … My heart is turned within Me; My compassion is stirred!” “Where, O Death, are your plagues? Where, O Sheol, is your sting?” The book ends in the dew: “I will be like the dew to Israel; he will blossom like the lily and take root like the cedars of Lebanon.”

The comic draws the prophet’s marriage as the heart of the book. Hosea’s house has one door: at 1:3 he brings Gomer in under a wedding garland hung on the doorframe; at 2:5 she walks out through the same door; at 3:3 he leads her, bought back, in through that same door, one hand guarding her back—all three times from the same camera angle. Gomer’s leaving is shown only by her back, the road beyond the door, and earrings someone else gave her; she is never drawn with her lovers. When she is bought back there are no ropes: the silver in the scale pan and the sacks of barley carry the panel. The children’s names are told with light: in the panel where the daughter is born, the light is drawing back out of the house; at “You are My people,” the three children look up in a wheat field. The preaching chapters take one image per page: the sower’s hand flings out a whirlwind, and a storm rolls in on the horizon; on one hillside the morning mist burns off and the dew dries, and at the end of the book, from the same angle, the whole slope stays wet with dew and covered in lilies—the only moist green in the book. God is never drawn in human form, not even a hand: “It was I who taught Ephraim to walk” shows only a toddler stepping across the desert sand with small hands outstretched toward a low warm light ahead; “How could I give you up” is the prophet’s door late at night, half open, a lamp on the threshold shining on an empty road, with no one in sight.

joel.title: Joel
joel.subtitle: The Promise of the Outpoured Spirit
intro: Joel was the son of Pethuel. The text never says under which king he spoke; all we can tell is that the temple in Jerusalem still stood and the priests still brought the grain and drink offerings. A plague of locusts swept over Judah wave after wave: “What the devouring locust has left, the swarming locust has eaten; what the swarming locust has left, the young locust has eaten; and what the young locust has left, the destroying locust has eaten.” The vines were ruined and the fig trees stripped of their bark—“the branches have turned white”—and even the grain and drink offerings were cut off from the temple. Joel tells the old men to pass it on—“Tell it to your children; let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation”—and calls to the priests, “Come, spend the night in sackcloth.” Then he sounds the ram’s horn in Zion and sees a greater day: “a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness. Like the dawn overspreading the mountains a great and strong army appears.” Here the book turns: “Yet even now,” declares the LORD, “return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning.” “So rend your hearts and not your garments.” The LORD is jealous for His land and promises, “I will repay you for the years eaten by locusts,” and then: “And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions.”—the very words Peter would quote at Pentecost. “And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved.” At the end the nations are brought down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat—“Beat your plowshares into swords”—“Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision!” Yet in that day “the mountains will drip with sweet wine, and the hills will flow with milk… a spring will flow from the house of the LORD.” The book closes on one line: “For the LORD dwells in Zion.”

The comic draws the locusts as real desert locusts: each one a lifelike insect, and in a swarm a cloud that blots out the sky. The text compares them to horses and warriors, and those stay comparisons—there are no monsters. Three things hold the book together. One field: green at the opening, eaten down to bare soil across four panels in a row by four waves of insects, and then, at “I will repay you for the years eaten by locusts,” the wheat comes back from the very same camera angle. One fig tree: stripped white, and later, from the same angle, heavy with leaves and fruit. One dark sky: sun and moon go dark three times, and the third time a single lamp burns on Mount Zion beneath it. The turning point of the book is 2:13: a hand gripping a collar to tear it stops, and presses against the chest instead. The pouring out of the Spirit is drawn the way Acts 2 is—no light, water, or fire falling from the sky, only people’s faces: a young bride speaking, a youth gazing into the distance, an old farmer smiling in his sleep. The plowshare bent into a sword under the hammer is struck on the same anvil as in Isaiah; the spring flowing from under the temple threshold at the end joins the river Ezekiel saw; and the last panel returns to the field from the opening, where the white-bearded farmer stands with his grandson beside the green wheat—“let your children tell it to their children.”

amos.title: Amos
amos.subtitle: Let Justice Roll On like a River
intro: Amos was “among the sheepherders of Tekoa”—a man of Judah sent to prophesy to the northern kingdom of Israel “two years before the earthquake, in the days when Uzziah was king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Jehoash was king of Israel,” the same generation as Hosea. These were the north’s richest years: palaces paneled with ivory rose on the hill of Samaria, and the crowds bringing sacrifices to the altar at Bethel were loud and cheerful. Amos opens with “The LORD roars from Zion and raises His voice from Jerusalem.” He begins with the nations: “For three transgressions of Damascus, even four, I will not revoke My judgment,” and then Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab, even Judah—the fire closes in ring by ring until it lands on his listeners themselves: “For three transgressions of Israel, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because they sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals.” He asks, “The lion has roared— who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken— who will not prophesy?” He calls the rich women of Samaria “cows of Bashan,” women “who oppress the poor and crush the needy.” Disaster follows disaster, and each one ends on the same words: “yet you did not return to Me,” until at last, “prepare to meet your God, O Israel!” He says, “Seek Me and live!” and then the heaviest line of the book: “But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.” As for those who “lie on beds inlaid with ivory”: “You drink wine by the bowlful and anoint yourselves with the finest oils, but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph.” Then come five visions: locusts, fire, a plumb line, a basket of summer fruit, the Lord beside the altar. Twice Amos pleads, “Lord GOD, please forgive!” and the disaster is stopped; the third time the LORD asks, “Amos, what do you see?” and he answers, “A plumb line,” and pleads no more. When Amaziah the priest of Bethel orders him back to Judah, he says, “I was not a prophet,” “nor was I the son of a prophet; rather, I was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees. But the LORD took me from following the flock.” He sees a famine coming, “not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the LORD.” Yet the book does not end in judgment: “In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David. I will repair its gaps”; “the plowman will overtake the reaper and the treader of grapes, the sower of seed. The mountains will drip with sweet wine”; “I will firmly plant them in their own land, never again to be uprooted from the land that I have given them.”

The comic draws Amos as a sunburned shepherd with rough hands: a coarse wool cloak in broad stripes of charcoal and undyed wool, a crook in his hand, and a small curved knife for tending sycamore-figs at his belt. God is never drawn in human form, nor as a lion—the “roar” is a thundercloud rolling over the summit of Carmel, the plumb line is a weighted cord hanging from the cloud against a leaning wall, and the Lord beside the altar is a single upright column of white light. Three things hold the book together. A ring of fire: through the eight oracles against the nations, the same small map sits in the corner of each panel and the fires light up one by one, while the crowd at the gate of Bethel grows happier and happier—until the panel on Israel, where the smiles freeze. A pair of sandals: silver on one side of the scales, an old pair of sandals on the other; the same barefoot poor man is pushed aside at the city gate and traded away on a grain merchant’s scales, and at the end of the book, wearing a new pair of sandals, he kneels to press down the soil around a newly planted vine. Ivory and the tent: the feast on ivory beds is the brightest, warmest panel of the book; later the tops of the pillars crack, and what is raised up again at the end is a plain shelter of branches. The five visions share one camera angle: twice Amos kneels to plead; the third time he stands and pleads no more. The heart of the book is 5:24: a great flood of water pours through the very gate where the poor were denied justice and overturns the judge’s scales. The field at the end of the book joins the end of Joel—“The mountains will drip with sweet wine.”

haggai.title: Haggai
haggai.subtitle: The Latter Glory of This House
intro: The book of Haggai is only two chapters long: four dated messages given within less than four months, beginning “In the second year of the reign of Darius, on the first day of the sixth month”—520 BC. The exiles who had returned had laid the foundation of the temple in Jerusalem and then stopped work for sixteen years; new houses went up in the city while grass grew over the foundation. Haggai brings the word of the LORD to Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest: “These people say, ‘The time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD.’” Then he asks, “Is it a time for you yourselves to live in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” “Consider carefully your ways. You have planted much but harvested little. You eat but never have enough … You earn wages to put into a bag pierced through.” The reason is a single sentence: “Because My house still lies in ruins, while each of you is busy with his own house.” “Go up into the hills, bring down lumber, and build the house”—and this time the people listened. Zerubbabel, Joshua, and “all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the LORD their God”; Haggai brings one short message, “I am with you,” and on the twenty-fourth day of the month “they came and began the work on the house of the LORD of Hosts, their God.” A month later, as old men who remembered Solomon’s temple looked at the new walls, the LORD asked through Haggai, “Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How does it look to you now? Does it not appear to you like nothing in comparison?” And then: “But now be strong, O Zerubbabel”; “My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid”; “The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine”; “The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former.” Before the winter rains Haggai asks them to remember the time “Before one stone was placed on another in the temple of the LORD,” when “one came expecting a heap of twenty ephahs of grain, there were but ten.” Then comes the turning point of the book: “Is there still seed in the barn? … But from this day on, I will bless you.” In the last message, given the same day, the LORD says, “I will overturn royal thrones,” and to Zerubbabel, “I will make you like My signet ring, for I have chosen you.”

The comic draws Haggai as an old prophet of about seventy—the same man who spoke on the overgrown foundation in Ezra: a white beard down to his chest, a coarse grey-brown camel-hair cloak, and a thick straight staff. Zerubbabel wears deep blue; Joshua the high priest wears his everyday white linen. Three things hold the book together. The same ring of white foundation stones: at the start the grass is knee-high and a wild goat lies beside the altar; later the wall rises course by course, and at the end scaffolding stands against it. Each message opens on the same wooden post standing on a foundation stone—blazing sun, falling rain, a puddle reflecting a breaking sky—so you can see at a glance that more days have passed. A year’s harvest: seed scattered by hand, a family that never has enough, pieces of silver dropping one by one from the bottom of a torn purse into the dirt; then in the winter rain the same field sprouts a row of green shoots, and a barefoot boy crouches down and looks up laughing. Houses: the prophet stands in a doorway, with a new house on his left—a cedar ceiling carved with palm trees, a family eating in the shade—and the deserted foundation on his right, where his staff is pointing. God is never drawn in human form: in 2:22 we see only the royal thrones toppled, the chariots overturned, the horses down in the dust. The heart of the book is 2:23: a gold signet ring engraved with a lion pressed into clay, and Haggai’s hand on Zerubbabel’s shoulder as Zerubbabel looks down at his own empty hand. The scaffolding at the end leads into the next book, Zechariah—the same year, the same people.
